headline: High-risk shared-file and MCP interaction: Semantic Kernel can read/write files and use MCP while the paired content source has broad egress, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent B can read/write filesystem and use MCP, so it may ingest Agent A-produced content if the pair shares files or plugins. Agent A is a content-writing source with broad network egress, so attacker-controlled or web-derived text could flow into B’s instruction path. No direct shared-channel evidence is present, so I avoid high.
conditions: IF Agent A output is copied into a file or MCP payload that Agent B reads as instructions
IF Agent B parses file contents or plugin responses without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of Agent A outputs into Agent B
Add provenance tags to all A→B content
Require a human review step before B executes instructions from files
Restrict B MCP plugins to allowlisted, read-only sources
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction/data separation

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent B explicitly reads and writes filesystem content and handles application context plus plugin credentials, while Agent A has broad network egress. If they share a workspace, B can expose A-originated files or context to external APIs. The profiles do not prove a shared workspace, so this is medium rather than high.
conditions: IF Agent A and Agent B share any filesystem or workspace
IF B sends file contents or application context to a third-party model provider or MCP server
mitigations: Separate A and B into different workspaces
Remove secrets from any shared directory
Turn off automatic file attachment in B
Use least-privilege credentials for B plugins
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent B can write files and use shared memory-store style state across instances; Agent A is a content-writing agent that may also emit files or artifacts through the surrounding workflow. That creates overlapping mutable-state risk if both touch the same workspace. Because Agent A has no explicit write surface in its profile, I do not escalate to high.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or shared memory store
IF the orchestrator does not provide locking or per-agent namespaces
mitigations: Assign separate output directories
Serialize writes with a lock file
Disable shared-state reuse between instances
Use per-agent namespaces for memory and artifacts
requires-engineering: add optimistic-concurrency conflict detection

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent B is a multi-agent orchestrator that can treat upstream outputs as inputs to plugins or other agents, so Agent A’s generated text can cascade into actions if not verified. Agent A is a content-writing source, making this pathway plausible. The profiles do not show explicit action authority, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF Agent B forwards Agent A output into a plugin or downstream agent without verification
IF B uses A-generated facts as authoritative prompts or tool arguments
mitigations: Insert a verification step before B consumes A output
Require citations for any factual claims passed onward
Limit B to read-only summarization of A output
Log all A→B handoffs for review
requires-engineering: add schema validation for inter-agent messages

E_compliance.rationale: No specific residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented for Agent A, while Agent B handles application context and plugin credentials but no regulated data class is named. With only docs-level evidence and no explicit compliance gap, the risk is limited to potential policy mismatch if sensitive data is introduced later.
conditions: IF regulated data such as PHI or EU PII is routed through Agent B
IF the deployment policy requires residency or retention guarantees not documented here
mitigations: Avoid routing regulated data through the pair
Review retention settings for B plugins
Document data-class handling before deployment
Restrict secrets to short-lived tokens
requires-engineering: obtain vendor compliance attestations
